subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 15. consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned last Tuesday I was referring to the resolution to ratify the Petersen contract, 'because to my mind there are aspects of similarity between it and this proposed bill. The Petersen contract was entered into by the government in 19125. It contained a laboured preamble that the government intended thereby to secure control of ocean freight rates, but it was plain to anyone who read the agreement that in the final analysis such control would be passed over to Sir William Petersen. Of course, it sounded fine to say to the members of this House: Oh, you are voting to give the government control of ocean freight rates, to put an end to a shippihg monopoly on the Atlantic. We struggled hard to impress upon the government that its claims were false and misleading, but they insisted that the contract must be regarded as almost inviolate. The then Minister of Trade and Commerce said: The contract is cast iron. The Prime Minister said:	We never would have made the
contract unless it entirely carried our judgment. What happened1? Against our protest the contract was referred to a special committee.
That committee laboured long over the matter and considering what was spent by the government and by those who were in attendance to give their views either for or against, probably, at least 8250,000 was expended in connection with the reference. When Sir William Petersen could not get what he thought was secured to him by the contract, by reason of the fact that the government could not secure its ratification by parliament, not only was the contract killed but its rejection involved his death.
Now, I do not imagine for a moment that the promoters of this bill may die in the committee room. But what has happened in the course of their efforts to secure its passage through this House? Every member has had the bill put before him as a measure which might mean-I will put it that way-which might mean the construction of a canal in the Georgian bay district. Nothing of the kind is intended. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) so acknowledges. He told us on Monday night that the issue involved was power, not a canal. He used the word "canal" only once in the whole course of his address, and then not to suggest that it was even a possibility. If I can do nothing else, Mr. Speaker, I want to register a strong protest against hon. members being hoodwinked and made fools of by promoters who lead us to believe that they want one thing when in reality they want something entirely different. The Right Hon. Winston Churchill has described that practice as the policy of "hugger mugger," and this certainly is an application of it. And hugger mugger he defines thus. When you want something very badly you have a grpat chance of success if you can fix in the public mind something else which the public desires very much and which you use as a cloak to cover the object you are after yourself. When you have well camouflaged your object then you try as vigilantly as you can to obtain it, and you may find in the end that you get what you want. I say it is beneath the dignity of this House and of every individual member of the House that a canal should even be mentioned or the possibility of its existence mooted in connection with this bill. Yet we have heard member after member from Alberta, 'Saskatchewan and Manitoba dealing with the Georgian bay canal and telling us how much the freight rates were going to be reduced.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to leave on the House an impression which possibly is not accurate. I do not think that any member from Alberta has supported the idea of building this canal.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
The mistake, Mr. Speaker, is absolutely mine. Possibly the members from Alberta belong to one of the cleverest sections of the House, and they are not prone to errors of that kind. Certainly, however, members from Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario who have been discussing this canal have suggested that as a result of its construction wheat would be moved at a cheaper rate, and they have also seen the vessels navigating this imaginary canal in less time and at less cost than other transportation lines operate. There are canals in Mars, so they tell us, and there are more chances of these members from Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario sailing on those Martian water-ways than on the Sifton canal which they have been talking about. I therefore object to this legislation being promoted in this House on the basis of the canal to be constructed. There is of course, in the bill not one word that has obviously to do with electrical energy, but that is the whole object of the bill. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) said, "Oh, well, this bill has been renewed from year to year fourteen times. Is it not very strange that those opposing it so very vigorously now should not have opposed its last renewal?" Here again I for one have to make a confession, which is something I do not like to do. This bill absolutely fooled me. I thought, when it came before the House in 1924, that it was really intended to build a canal, or that at any rate somebody was lingeringly thinking of a canal. I do not believe there was any such object in view at that time, and I am the more confirmed in this opinion by the fact that the bill of '1924 contained a saving clause which protected the rights of the country. That clause is omitted from the bill now before us, and that omission leaves the bill absolutely one of power and not one that aims at the construction of a canal. That saving clause, which was enough to disarm anyone, provided that the government of Canada could, on one week's notice, take over the whole enterprise, assume possession of it, enjoy its property, and this by paying merely the value thereof. That, clause, I find, is left out of this bill and the omission, I maintain, has made the power feature the only object of this legislation. If the promoters of the bill spend $50,000 they have nine years in which to lay hold of and control every horsepower of electrical energy that can be developed upon the Ottawa and French rivers, provided always that the provinces have not exclusive jurisdiction. The gist of the bill-and no one can deny it-is that the expenditure of $50,000 gives to these private interests, so 
far as the government of Canada is concerned, the right to develop all the power they possibly can in the nine years, to the whole extent of the 1.000,000 horse-power. Then what happens? The husk of the charter in the shape of the canal proposal falls away, and these interests are absolutely confirmed by our legislation in the sole control and ownership of that immense value in electrical energy. When we find a bill involving such consequences inimical to the interests of the country, it is our duty to administer a reproof to those who promote such a bill. It is our duty to defeat it rather than aid its progress through this House.
While I do not like even to mention the word canal as a possibility in connection with this legislation, I would point out that in 1914 there was appointed by the government a commission consisting of Mr. W. Sanford Evans and two other gentlemen to investigate the practicability of the whole Georgian bay canal project. That commission reported. I know very well the gentleman who acted as its chairman, a man who lives and has lived' for a number of years in the west, who understands the wheat trade probably as well as any man in Canada and who is familiar with the transportation problems that face that trade. The report was made by the commission to the effect that this canal was not feasible and would never be an advantage to the farmers in the way anticipated by Sir Robert Perks and those who advocated the canal. It was further reported that nothing could be gained by a canal of this description even if it could be built, and the whole thing passed out of the picture. No reference has been made to that report by anyone now pretending to be interested in the canal. The minister did not refer to it when he spoke the other evening, and no member of the government, not one of the promoting party, has seen fit to controvert or even to mention the report of that commission. I say, therefore, that so long as that report stands unanswered, the possibilty of this canal becomes even more remote than it was before. And that is so far off that its distance would have to be measured, as great distances are measured, by so many light years-again reaching the regions beyond Mars.
Some of us were quite interested in what was said by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) the other evening. He has been criticized by the Toronto Globe, which as every one knows is not a paper which as a rule supports the Conservative party, for having played small politics in his address to the House, and I think he left a false impression upon the House which I hope to be able to correct. The lease entered into in 1921

Georgian Bay Canal Company
was referred to and condemned, and I want to draw attention to the fact that after condemning the 1921 lease and after condemning in perhaps stronger terms the 1926 lease he told us that the government of which he is a member renewed that 1921 lease for five months, and it is in existence to-day. If that lease was improper, which was the impression given, then it was the duty of this government and of the minister who claims it was improper to cancel it at the first opportunity; that was not done and it is in existence at this very moment. This fact, it seems to me, robs the attack of the Minister of Railways of much of its sting. He went on further to say that the lease entered into' in 1926 was ill-timed; why? Because it was negotiated about three months in advance of the time when the existing lease fell in. The minister left the impression that this was done because of the near election. The lease expired on December 1, the men concerned in that lease are at least business men, and three months was all too short a time in which to make arrangements to prevent cutting off the consumers of power in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. But the minister said also that the lease of 1926 contained a clause which meant that $600,000 of the money of the people of Canada was given up for the benefit of the lessees. What does that mean? The lease runs for eighty years, which means about $7,500 a year and if the minister examines the matter he will find the reduction in the price of power was made in consideration of the term of the lease. The first lease was for five years and the second for eighty years, and a reduction was demanded and given to the consumers to the amount of $7,500 a year. The consumers got the benefit of it, but the impression left with the House was that the lessees realty benefited.
In the next place the minister made a great play out of the alleged fact that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec were each to receive one-third of the rental, in case the rental was reduced. To put it more clearly, it will be remembered that there are two disputed claims to the power; the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have their rights and this Dominion is asserting its right. It is claimed that all the power belongs to the provinces but the Dominion has made an agreement whereby the rental is paid to it, and this clause which the minister attacked merely provided that in case Ontario and Quebec established their rights and exacted payment of the rental to them, by so much as the rental had to be paid to the provinces-the Dominion would abate. That is only fair; if it turned out that the
provinces were by law entitled to collect the rent, the Dominion would have to be satisfied with that condition. There is no complaint that the provinces are not parties to this lease; it would not be artistic draftsmanship or conveyancing if they were parties to it. They make their separate arrangements and the Dominion makes its arrangement, but at the time these leases were entered into the provinces were consulted, and my information is that on the last occasion, in August of 1926, both the provinces of Ontario and Quebec were satisfied with and desired the lease which was entered into. The minister said, "Oh, a lease of this valuable property was given for eighty years, until the year 2006." That is only about twice as long as this charter has kicked around this House and further, if the principle of this bill is adopted on second reading it is not only giving away 300,000 horse-power until 2006, but it is giving away 1,000,000 horse-power to the Sifton interests forever. That, it seems, is what the minister advocates. The principle of this bill now before us gives the power to be developed under it, so far as the Dominion has the right to do so, to these interests forever; whatever is in their hands at the end of nine years belongs absolutely and forever to the promoters of this bill. When the matter is looked at in that way I think it will be seen that instead of an improvident lease having been made, those who acted with the consent and approval of the provinces were acting in the interests of the Dominion of Canada as well. If there is a disputed title; if the provinces claim all and that claim is sustained, in any case the Dominion of Canada will have a one-third interest. It may very well be that the courts and the Privy Council, if it goes that far, will decide the proportions should be different, but I fail to see how it can be proved that the provinces are not entitled to at least two-thirds of the water-power developed by what has been already held to be their water. Therefore it seems to me that the care taken by those acting at the time in the right of the Dominion of Canada has been absolutely justified by the results.
What happens now? We have the contract which was made by the Conservative government approved by the Liberal government; we have this question of power, with its uncertainty as to title and right; we have the government of the day saying, through the Minister of Railways, that this matter must be brought to the attention of parliament. It is now before parliament; it is certainly within the power of the government to investigate anything that may be in any
Georgian Bay Canal Company

shape or form supposed to be not in accordance with the very right and justice of the case nor in the interests of the country. But what has not been done, and I submit should not be done, is to investigate, as the Minister of Railways has proposed, a question of this kind upon a reference to a standing committee in the case of a private bill. The promoter of a private bill is supposed to look after the passage of that bill, is he not? Why does the Minister of Railways wish to investigate public matters upon a private bill that has no reference on its face to the subject of the investigation? I submit that the reference would not be wide enough to include any such subject as the minister hinted he was anxious to investigate. The minister said that the matter only became of great national and .provincial importance when it was found that this lease, the latter one, had been cancelled by the government. I submit that plainly that is not the reason why such newspapers, flaming evangels of the Liberal cause, as the Ottawa Citizen, the Toronto Globe, and the Brantford Expositor are telling this government that at the first opportunity this bill should be thrown out of the House. And newspapers in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, as well as in all parts of Canada, have said that this bill should be given no consideration whatever. I cannot understand how anyone living in the province of Ontario who has been accustomed to hear what is said by men who have benefited from the development of hydro-electric power in the province could imagine for a moment that the people of that province would brook any interference at the present time with what they consider their rights to power and the further development of power. There is no county in the province of Ontario except possibly, and only possibly, the two very far eastern counties, and I would not even except them, where anyone can stand up and say that he is opposed to what has been accomplished by the province of Ontario in the development of hydro-electric power. They want to see that good work go on, they are determined that it shall go on; and no question of party politics, no public issue that I know of, no other issue of any kind, ranks in importance with the determination of the people that hands shall be kept off the development of power in the public interest. That is the reason for my opposition to this bill.
I object to the bill in the first place, because it is false and misleading in character as I have explained. I object to it in the second place because it is against the interests of the Dominion of Canada so far as the federal authority has the right to deal

with this power. I object to it in the third place because if the Dominion does insist that it has a claim to this power, it will mean that litigation will take place, time will be consumed, and money will be expended and I believe not to the benefit of the people. I object to giving this bill a second reading also because the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, as I have said, are united in opposing it. I am told that Premier Taschereau of Quebec has intimated to-day that he stands wholeheartedly with the premier of the province of Ontario against this legislation. If that is the case, and the government can easily ascertain the fact, why should it not respect the will of the people? How often have we heard declarations from horn, gentlemen opposite that the will of the people ought to be allowed to take effect. I say that the overwhelming will of the people is against this bill, is against giving it a second reading.
In conclusion I want merely to read a short extract from the Toronto Globe of today, to the following effect:
But does the Georgian Bay Company think for one moment that members of the Canadian parliament are so stupid as to be misled by the stress placed on the canal feature of the charter? Does it not realize that everyone knows that no corporation will sink millions of dollars in an enterprise which, on the face of it, cannot be a financial success? So why does it not come out in the open and say that it wants the people's power rights, which would make the charter worth hundreds of millions of dollars, and without which the charter would be useless?
The people know this, the members of parliament know it, the ministry knows it. The question is not whether the Sifton interests shall get authority to build a canal, but whether they shall get the power; and on this there can be no compromise. They cannot get this power unless the government throws the weight of its votes and influence with them. Does the government dare do it? Will Mr. King risk the honour of the Liberal party and the political life of his Ontario ministers and members by thwarting the expressed wish of the people of this province? Would his chief cabinet minister, the Minister of Finance, who has rightly earned the confidence of the country for honesty and rectitude, permit the heritage of the provinces to be diverted to private interests? Would any cabinet minister at Ottawa tolerate such an abuse of public rights?
The day has passed when the people's interests can be disregarded with impunity. The sooner the federal government lets the electors know that it realizes this, the sooner will it clear itself of the suspicion which now hangs over it in the matter of a great public utility franchise.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I
presume there is very little I can add to the discussion which has already taken place on this bill, but I fear, Sir, I would be negligent in my duty as a member of this House and

Georgian Bay Canal Company
I would not be true to the responsibility I owe to my constituents did I not place myself on record as being opposed to the measure that we are now considering. I have frer quently during this debate heard arguments from across the way that, whether we are in favour of the bill or not, no harm could come by sending it to a committee, that we should at least be fair and permit the bill to go to a committee and there hear all the arguments for and against it. It seems to me a rather ridiculous thing that if we are opposed to the very principle of the bill, if we are opposed to the very principles of granting water-powers to private interests, we should provide a means of taking up the time of members by sending the bill to a committee. I can hardly conceive of any member who really objects to that principle being in favour of taking that course. To my mind if one objects to that principle now is the proper time to raise the objection. Therefore I cannot understand the argument or the line of talk we have heard so much in this debate to the effect that whether we are in favour of the bill or not we should at least permit it to go to committee.
Now, Sir, my reasons for opposing this bill are, in the first place, because the waterpower will be required by the people of Ontario. Of course it can be said, and it has been said in this debate, that whether these water-powers be developed by the Ontario Hydro Electric, or whether they be developed by private interests, the people will have the use of the power just the same. But, Sir, there is a vast difference between a public utility' owned and controlled by the people of the province of Ontario, and one in the hands of a group of capitalists who will make all the money out of it they possibly can, and assess industry, and assess the householders who are obliged to use the power, all the traffic will bear. The Ontario Hydro Electric Commission now control, I understand, about 900,000 horse-power, and they have an investment of $240,000,000. On this basis it is authoritatively estimated that the 1,250,000 horse-power that this bill would give to these private interests would be worth a capitalization of not less than half a billion dollars, an enormous sum. It is proposed to put into the hands of these private capitalists the power to assess the people of Ontario and Quebec for all time to come, and to hinder in various ways the development of industry in those provinces. Of course the argument is used that the Quebec share of this would, under the policy adopted by the provincial government, be handed over in any event to private interests.
But that is not our concern; our business is to deal with this matter on our responsibility as the House of Commons of Canada. Once those water-powers are turned over to the provinces we have nothing more to say. If the Quebec government desires to turn those water-powers over to private rather than public interests, that is the business of the people of that province. On the other hand, if the Ontario government, representing the people of that province, desire that the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission should control this power, that is their business, and it is not for us to put anything in their way.
The Ontario legislative assembly has put itself on record unanimously as being opposed to this bill. Liberals, Conservatives and Progressives have joined to the last man in the Ontario legislature in opposing it. Ottawa is a city right on this wonderful waterway by which the enormous quantity of wheat we heard about was going to be transported to the Atlantic, a city, one would think, that would benefit greatly by the development of this canal. Yet we find the council of the city of Ottawa unanimously condemning this proposition and passing a resolution to that effect.
We have heard frequently during this debate that the western farmers are in favour of the construction of this canal. How often have we heard that old cryl Whenever some privileged interest wants something from this House, it is always for the benefit of the western farmer, and he is frequently invoked to support it. I would call on any of these hon. gentlemen who use that argument to show me a single instance, to quote a single statement by any one representing any body of farmers, or by any body of farmers in western Canada, showing that they have placed themselves on record as being in favour of the construction of this canal. The farmers of western Canada realize that we have already spent enormous sums of money on transportation. In addition to the already expensive canal system that we have from the head of the lakes to Montreal, we are now opening up the Hudson bay route. Some years ago we spent $170,000,000 on a transcontinental railway designed for the express purposes of giving the western farmers the shortest and best possible route by rail to the sea. But we are effectively prevented from using that route. So far as actual effect is concerned, the government of this country, or the Board of Railway Commissioners, or whoever is responsible, might just as well have built a brick wall across the transcontinental in order to prevent us from using it.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Nevertheless in spite of that we propose to spend an enormous sum of money in developing another route to the sea.
Of course we have heard frequently from protagonists of this bill that no public money is involved; that a group of private capitalists are going to construct this canal; that they are going to put up all the money. But it is really immaterial whether we provide the money out of the public treasury for the construction of this canal or give them water-powers worth half a billion dollars. I would much rather see a company come to parliament and ask for a subsidy to construct a waterway of that nature, because then we would know just what we were dealing with.
Cf course, that is all on the assumption that there is going to be a canal. I think, however, it is generally understood that this is not the purpose of the promoters at ali; that they will never construct a canal; the only object to be served is to obtain control of these valuable water-powers. I wonder if ail hon. members realize the relationship that exists to-day between water-power and industry. I wonder if they realize the dominant position that in the future may be held by Canada in the markets of the world in regard to manufactured goods. In another twenty-five years, if we retain these water-powers and use them wisely and judiciously so that industry will be able to obtain the cheapest possible power, we are going to put our manufacturers in a position almost to control the markets of the world, because every day it is becoming more and more obvious that the country which a quarter of a century from now controls its own water-powers will hold a dominant position in the markets of the world in regard to manufactured' products. Therefore, Canada's attainment of that proud position in another twenty-five years will be determined by whether or not we decide to conserve and hold these water-powers for the benefit of future generations. We are legislating to-day not for those who are here at present, but for countless millions of Canadians yet unborn, Canadians who will look back and either condemn or bless us according to the way in which we handle this great heritage that should be preserved for our children and our children's children.
Several hon. members from Manitoba have placed themselves very strongly on record as being in favour of this bill. Of course that is not a difficult matter to explain when one goes back to western Canada. It can be said that after all we were dealing with something that

was an issue in Ontario. It would not be an important matter to tell my constituents that we gave away water-powers in that way in Ontario. The issue would not be a direct one there; but to be fair and to look at this question from a natural standpoint, I would ask some of these hon. gentlemen from Manitoba to change the geographical description in this bill and to make it apply to the northern part of their province. Let us imagine to-night that we are considering a bill which proposes to canalize the Nelson river to its mouth. That ambitious project was at one time actually discussed and very seriously considered in the city of Winnipeg. The idea was to make Winnipeg an ocean port, and it was believed that the water-power that was on that great river would more than pay for the expense of canalization; that Winnipeg would then be an ocean port, and that we could deliver our grain from the city of Winnipeg by water right to the open sea. That was the ambitious project that was considered about forty or forty-five years ago in the city of Winnipeg. After all it is not such a dream and indeed some time in the future it may come true. Engineers sent out there by the Dominion government have estimated that there is no less than 6,000,000 horse-power capable of being developed on the Nelson river. That river, as we know, is one of the greatest in the world, and its vast potentialities to the province of Manitoba, can hardly yet be estimated, but some day in the future that water-power will be harnessed, and it will be developing countless industries in the province of Manitoba. It will be delivering power to the farmers of the province and to the householders in the small towns, and it will put the province of Manitoba in an entirely different position from what it occupies to-day in regard both to industry and agriculture. Indeed, I think the time will come, and perhaps before very long, when the city of Winnipeg will be one of the greatest manufacturing centres on the North American continent. That seems a dream to-day, but with these immense water-powers right at her door, and with the newer transmission developments that enable the movement of power over long distances without serious loss, it seems to me that the day will come, and before very long, when the city of Winnipeg will be one of the greatest manufacturing centres on this continent. When we come to the day when we shall need all these water-powers developed, if they have been already coralled by private capitalists, who will simply charge all the traffic will bear, what is that going to mean to the province of Manitoba? We are either

Private Bilk
going to develop enormous industries there, or with these water-powers in the hands of private capital industry will be stifled from the very beginning. I would appeal to my hon. friends from Manitoba just to visualize the effect of this bill as applied to their own province, as applied to those enormous water-powers on the Nelson and Winnipeg rivers, and let them imagine for one moment the wave of popular indignation that would sweep not only over the province of Manitoba but over the whole of the west if there was any attempt on the part of this parliament to alienate those resources for all time to come. I ask my hon. friends to take that into consideration before they vote to send this bill to the committee.
I say again that I am opposed to the very principle of this bill, and that being so, I can see nothing to be gained from sending it to the committee. Therefore I intend to vote against it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock we were considering the new rule to be added after rule 21, limiting speeches to forty minutes. Mr. Neil'l had moved to add to this rule the words, " except on a budget debate". Shall the amendment carry?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Might I take this opportunity to correct a slight misunderstanding that occurred this afternoon between myself and the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards)? He asked me if I could think of a situation where there would be a province with only'- one representative, and I did not catch his question. I was referring to a case where there might 'be sixteen members from a province, fifteen of one particular stripe of politics and the other of the opposite stripe, that the party to which the fifteen adhered might bring in something prejudicially affecting the interests of the (province, and that the duty of combating the proposal would devolve on that one representative. I was not referring to a case like the Yukon.
In defence of the proposed new rule an hon. member explained this afternoon that there were no less than sixteen opportunities to speak on the budget. If you multiply sixteen by forty, you get a total of ten hours and forty minutes, if a member took advantage of his opportunity. Where is the saving of time? In the one case he makes sixteen speeches consuming ten hours and forty minutes, but in the other case his physical limitations would stop him long before he had spoken for that length of time. If it will not make any difference, why pass the rale?

Rules oj the House

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A money bill cannot be
passed two stages at the same sitting without unanimous consent. So at one sitting a member could speak forty minutes and repeat his performance the day after until the bill was disposed of. Consequently I dio not think we are curtailing a member's right in any way. This simply means that he cannot speak for more than forty minutes at a time.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I appreciate the point made
by the hon. gentleman, but dividing a speech into sixteen sections seems to me something like dividing your prayers into sixteen portions. It has been suggested that this new rule will shorten debate and stop obstruction. Will it? We have an instance at the present time in the opposition to the Georgian bay canal bill. I do not think I can be accused of imputing improper motives by terming the opposition "obstruction", because the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) said more than once in the course of his speech against the bill: "I am here to talk it out."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Did you ever do that?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Sure-when I thought the
occasion justified it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is what we are doing
in this case.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not objecting to hon.
members opposite taking advantage of the rules; that is their privilege. But supposing the speeches had been confined to forty minutes-and most of them were made within this time-it would not have prevented obstruction. It would only mean putting up more men each to talk forty minutes instead of a few occupying the attention of the House for a hundred minutes each. It would be something like the Irishman who pondered whether he would save a million dollars in one j^iar or accomplish the same purpose by saving one dollar a year for a million years.
I heartily agree with the remarks made by my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) when he put his finger on the cause of a good deal of waste of time in connection with the estimates. I have noticed exactly what the hon. gentleman has described. A minister will patiently explain an item half a dozen times, and then someone who has not taken the trouble to be in his seat saunters in and starts the thing all over again. If the minister, somewhat harrassed, answers sharply, that member immediately begins to whine and complain how difficult it is to get a civil answer to a civil question. There are other difficulties. A member speaks for a minute or two and sits down and someone else jumps
up and discusses a totally different phase of the subject. More time is wasted in that way in committee than in reasonably lengthy
speeches.
As regards the forty minute proposition, as the hon. member for Lisgar pointed out, no allowance is made for interruptions. Give a man a couple of untenable points of order and a couple of irrelevant questions that throw him off the track and you waste so much of his time that his speech will not amount to very much. It may be said that allowance will be made for this, but it is not expressed in the rules. If it were, matters would be different. A man might raise a point of order on very slim grounds and so take up a good deal of the time of the member speaking. Someone might see a fancied insinuation in the speaker's remarks and raise a point which might consume fifteen minutes. Someone else asks a fool question that takes up ten minutes or more. It may be contended, .of course, that no one is bound to answer; but there are circumstances under which a man is bound to do so if he does not want to rest under an undeserved odium. Suppose a member were advocating a certain railway line and someone asked, "Is it not a fact that you are being paid by the railway company to promote this bill?" Can that member allow such a question to pass unheeded? Of course not; if he did the newspapers next day would come out with a headline, "Member accused of being paid servant of company and sits dumb under accusation". There are occasions, I say, on which a man, either through courtesy or of necessity, must reply to interruptions. Allow four such interruptions as I have suggested'- and there is nothing abnormal about the suggestion, for these interruptions do occur- and how much of the forty minutes ha3 he left?
The closure has been advocated, and it is said that is even a more extreme form of preventing debate. But there is this difference between the closure and the method proposed in this rule: the restriction of free speech by means of curtailing the time allotted to any member is imposed automatically by this rule, whereas in the case of closure notice must be given by the government, who must assume the responsibility before the country. If the government abuse the closure method, they must answer to the people. There is therefore no danger in that direction. As a matter of fact there is no record in any of the countries in which the closure is practised of this method having been seriously abused, and that for the very reason I mention, of the responsibility which the government assumes

Rules of the House

in imposing it. This little private rule of ours, however, would be invoked automatically without any responsibility on the part of the government or of any member of the government.
I come now to another point of interest apropos of the situation. Let me ask hon. members from the maritime provinces what they consider the most important piece of legislation before parliament this session. Is it not the matters involved in the Duncan report? Would those hon. gentlemen like this resolution to come into force at once, every one of them being limited to a forty minute speech on that important report? That, I think, is a good illustration of the danger I am pointing out in connection with a rule of this kind.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We will accept these
regulations in toto to-night.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman willing to accept them?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend speak for the Whole party?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was not asked to speak for the party. The hon. member wondered whether anyone from the maritime provinces would be content to deal with the Duncan report under the forty minute limitation. My reply is, I am prepared to accept all these regulations in toto to-night.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Then I apologize to the hon. gentleman. I gave him credit for more devotion to his province than he appears to have.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The case of my province is so clear that I can state it in fifteen minutes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I foresee another result Which will follow from this rule. The rule will lead to speeches being written out and rattled off as speedily as possible, and in this I anticipate a great advantage to the hon. member for Fort William. Why should that hon. member be given an advantage over all the rest of us? It is to handicap those less ably endowed than he, and it is not fair. There should be some sort of handicap imposed upon him. Again, Mr. Chairman, it is a notorious fact that the best speeches are not those that have been written out and that are read off. Most of the best speeches are delivered from notes, or without any such help at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: And they are not the longest, either.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are often not as long as the others. Now, how are we to ascertain
fMr. Neill.]
how long any given speech must be in order to come within the compass of the time allowed? The only way that can possibly be determined is for the member to have his speech typewritten and then read off to someone who holds a stop-watch to time him. Will the stenographic staff be equipped with stopwatches, and shall we be Obliged to read our speeches to the stenographers in order to ascertain whether they can be crammed into thirty-nine or forty minutes? And will there be any extra compensation to the staff for the added work in this direction? Why, Mr. Chairman, the result will be simply this: either this rule will be abused or it will be ignored altogether. I do not know what will happen, but either of these things will be the result. The chances are tlhat as time goes on the rule will be practically ignored, and if that is the case, what is the use of adopting it. At any rate, I predict one or other of these consequences. An hon. member reminds me that my time is nearly up. Well, for once in my life let me exceed the time limit.
I am perfectly serious about this subject, notwithstanding that it has its humorous aspect. There will be a reaction in the country to . the imposition of such a rule as this. The people will have a feeling something of this character: "We sent these men to Ottawa to represent us and express our views. We paid them to go there and speak for us"-because after all, to put it bluntly, we are paid to come here

"and now they are shirking their responsibility." That is not tTue, I know, but that is what the people will fancy. I say, there will be a reaction to this rule and we shall be suspected of shirking our responsibility.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the hon. member assume that members who do not speak forty minutes necessarily Shirk their responsibility?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, perhaps they serve their
purpose by listening. As Milton says, "They also serve who only stand and wait." I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we could better deal with the problem by an appeal to our dignity, to our esprit de corps. I have not the resolution before me, but it is in my recollection that years ago a motion was passed in this House with reference to lengthy speeches containing voluminous quotations and involving a waste of time. This practice was deplored and the resolution went on to recommend to members that they abstain from the propensity to being so long-winded. It did have the desired effect on those members to whom it was addressed and who have since ceased to belong to the House. I suggest an appeal

Rules oj the House
to the common sense and the sense of dignity of the House. Let hon. gentlemen try to cut down the length of their speeches. An appeal of that sort, I am sure, would be more effective than any hard and fast rule such as is now proposed. W hat we should be guided by in this connection is what has characterized the British constitution, which is founded almost entirely upon precedent rather than upon the letter of any rule-precedent broadening down to precedent. The statement was made not long ago that if we endeavoured to put into legal language the bonds that bind the dominions of the empire together, it would be exceedingly difficult to secure unity. That is true, and we should try to keep it in mind. We are trying to make hard and fast rules when it would be better to leave it to the good sense and judgment of the members of the House. Are we going to accuse ourselves of being lacking in good sense, good taste and good judgment? The amendment I have proposed is very simple; if I might explain it, it is intended to allow members to speak as long as they think necessary on only one occasion during the course of each session; that is, on the budget. The budget covers a large number of subjects, and I do not think the dignity of parliament will be at all endangered if once in the course of each session a member is allowed to speak as long as he wishes. If we find that this still materially handicaps parliament we can change it another year, but I would suggest that we are passing a lot of very drastic rules to-day some of which we do not understand and will not appreciate until later on, and I think we are going too far altogether when we limit the right of free speech.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am going to take the
liberty for a few moments of giving the reasons why I range myself in this matter beside the Minister of Justice and others who served on the committee in favour of forty minute speeches. It is not, as my hon. friend has said, because I ordinarily speak so rapidly, but because I believe it would enhance the value of our debates if they were boiled down. Someone has well said, and it has often been repeated, that brevity is the soul of wit, and I do think that most of our speeches would be improved by being shortened and by doing away with a lot of these excrescences of which we are all guilty at times, particularly if we have not given proper time to the preparation of our remarks.
This afternoon as I listened to the debate without participating in it, I remembered having read some years ago a book by Lord Curzon on parliamentary eloquence, which I
have since looked up to check my memory. In that book the author discussed eloquence from the speeches of the different speakers he had heard and some which he had just read, and he gave as one of the three greatest masterpieces of English eloquence the Gettysburg speech by Lincoln, which has been quoted again and again as perhaps the greatest masterpiece of eloquence in the English language. Some years ago I timed myself in reading that speech, and I find that it takes about a minute and a half to read it all.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: But we are not all Lincolns.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, we are not, but I do not know that my hon. friend had to say that. I remember that the author quoted at the same time what he considered the three great masterpieces of literature, two of them speeches by Lincoln and one a speech by William Pitt. The second speech by Lincoln was his second inaugural address, which was very brief, while the masterpiece by William Pitt consisted of only three lines. When great master pieces of eloquence can be made in such a brief time, it seems to me that forty minutes should be long enough for those of us who, like my good friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) are not Lincolns. We should be happy to take less than forty minutes even, and so boil down our addresses. It seems to me that we might even go further in this resolution, and put some time limit on the debates. When we take a month or six weeks, as has been the case in a number of the eleven sessions I have been in the House, in debating either the speech from the throne or the budget, I think we are taking altogether too much time; I think we might well make the limit a week or ten days in a dress debate of any kind. However, that is not before us at present, and I do not intend to press it, but I think everyone who has been in this House for several sessions will agree that on those occasions when the closure has been put in force and speeches have been limited to twenty minutes, we have heard addresses of the very best type, cut down to that- length of time.
Since my good friend from Comox-Alberni took me into account, Mr. Chairman, I just wished to place myself on record as against his amendment and as favourable to the report of the committee, because I think if we can lessen the length of our speeches, cut down the duration of the sessions and make the sacrifices of public men a little less than they are at present, we will build up the whole character of our parliamentary institutions.
Rules of the House

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was very much disposed to oppose the adoption of this rule, but felt that it would foe useless to do so after the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) spoke in opposition to it, because in opposing it he has given a very good demonstration of why it should be adopted. It took the hon. gentleman twenty-five minutes to express his views in respect to this question, and I can understand why he particularly does not want any limit placed on the budget debate. If it takes him twenty-five minutes on a little rule like this it would take him about twenty-five weeks to express his views on a subject like the budget. The hon. gentleman suggested that this limit should not apply to the budget debate and as I understood him his reason was that he is in a class by himself from the province of British Columbia, so far as the budget is concerned. He therefore thinks that he in particular should have a little more latitude than other people.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is twelve to one.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. Well, if you apply that principle, and accept the argument that these various groups should be recognized, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would be able to speak on the budget as long as he pleased, because he is the only one from British Columbia holding the peculiar views to which he subscribes. The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) should then have unlimited time also, because she represents all the women in the Dominion of Canada.
I was rather struck with the argument of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), who argued strongly against this forty minute rule. The way he would handle the matter is this: He would refer it to the whips and let them limit the time and make a selection of the men who should speak. That is nothing but the application of closure through the medium of the whips, and I object most strongly to it. I presume the reason why exception is made in the case of the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition, a minister moving a government order, a member speaking immediately in reply to such minister, a member making a motion of no confidence in the government and a minister replying thereto is because, in the case of the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition and other ministers, of their lack of experience in public speaking; they possibly need a little more time than others in which to express their views. If that is not the reason I do not know what it can be un-
(Mr. Manion.]
less it is that the matter is of so much importance that they should have special regulations.
The hon. member for Comox-Albemi argued that this rule should not apply to the budget debate, but might I point out in opposition to that suggestion that if an exception is made in that case certainly other matters will come up of even greater importance than the budget. I venture to say that many hon. members of this House regard the Duncan report, for instance, as of greater importance so far as this session is concerned than the budget debate, and why we should make an exception in the case of the budget and not in other matters I cannot possibly understand. What I particularly wish to say is this:	If
an exception is made to this rule in regard to the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition and certain other members mentioned, although I am not prepared to agree that an exception should be made, then it does seem to me that the exception should be carried a little further in order to apply to any member who introduces a resolution; such a member should have a little more than forty minutes in which to lay his case before parliament. On the order paper this session, for instance, there are a number of motions standing in the names of different hon. gentlemen, many of which are of great importance. I can readily understand why it might be somewhat difficult for a member introducing one of these subjects to cover the ground as it should be covered in the space of forty minutes. I am not arguing against the rule of forty minutes if it is applied all round, but I do say that there are subjects on the order paper before us which would indicate to me that private members under certain circumstances, should be exempted from the application of this rule just as much as these who are especially named for exemption. I believe the idea of cutting down or limiting the length of speeches is a very good one, and I take no particular exception to it, but I think it should be applied all round and made applicable to every membeT, ministers as well as others.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I disagree most
heartily with the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and to oppose the amendment which he has submitted to the House. We have heard the honest expression by His Honour the Speaker this afternoon that the very best speeches delivered in this chamber were only of twenty minutes duration and given under the closure. I think we should attach a good

Rules oj the House
deal of importance to a statement such as that coming from the gentleman who presides over the deliberations of this chamber, and who was the chairman of the committee that revised these rules. In the past the practice has been to talk for an indefinite period. Those of us who have been in the House for the past few years have listened sometimes to speeches which occupied two hours, even three hours, and I recall an instance of a private member speaking for three hours and forty minutes. It is quite true that member did not stay within the borders of his own province nor within the confines of the Dominion itself; in fact I think he girdled the earth from east to west. In several instances I doubt very much if it was possible to follow him in all the remarks that he made.
Now the amendment as proposed by the committee is to limit speeches to forty minutes. I think the amendment does not go quite far enough. If the best speeches that have been delivered in this House only occupied twenty minutes why should we extend the time to forty minutes? Personally I would favour cutting it down to thirty minutes. I think any person who has little or much to say, and who has his subject well in hand, should be able to present his ideas in thirty minutes. Perhaps the most of us attend church service occasionally, and if the preacher were to occupy more than thirty minutes in the delivery of his sermon we would be very much dissatisfied. As a matter of fact if a preacher extends his sermon beyond half an hour he finds his congregation getting up and walking out, indicating that he takes too long. Now I rather think that the thoughts to which a preacher gives expression are just as good and just as necessary as the ideas advanced by a lot of members of this House-in fact they are more necessary.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does the hon.
member advocate applying the rule of closure to ministers?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The closure is applied when members of the congregation get up and walk out.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is the
very point of the discussion to-night.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Perhaps the most
important speech delivered this session was the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, yet it took him only thirty-five minutes to deliver it. If the budget speech, covering taxation proposals for the whole Dominion, can be presented in that length of time, why should any mere member of parliament need
more than even half an hour to present the needs of his constituency? It is true that any of us could take more than half an hour. A member could speak for an hour and a half and say no more than he could say in half an hour, but that is not a legitimate reason for insisting upon the longer period of time It would be a good deal better to have an expression of opinion by several members in the same space of time that such a speech occupies. In the case of the member who spoke for three hours and forty minutes a couple of years ago, if there had been a limit of half an hour we could have had seven speeches in that period of time. Surely in a budget debate it would be much more preferable to have the opinions of seven members from different portions of the country than simply to have the opinion of one individual delivered at such length. Therefore I would be very much opposed to the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi. I would prefer there should be a thirty minute maximum, but I presume the committee have considered the matter from all angles, and perhaps the limit fixed in the proposed rule is a compromise, although I do not know as to that. A forty minute limit is better than none at all, and certainly if you had such a limit it should apply to the budget debate in which there a re speeches of such great length.
There is another matter in connection with the proposed rule as to which there should be an amendment. I do not know that it would be in order at the present moment, but possibly when the amendment we are considering is voted down, as I expect it will be, the amendment I have in mind would be in order. It is with reference to the position of those who are privileged to represent groups in the House. The proposed rule recognizes only the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, thus giving- recognition to two groups merely. I would not go to the extent of saying that we should recognize every group here no matter what their numerical strength might be, but we should take some notice of existing conditions. It does seem to me that when opinions are expressed by the government side of the House, which is supposed to be low tariff, and then opinions are expressed by the opposition side, which is supposed to be high tariff, although we know there is not so very much difference between the two, then there should be an expression of opinion by the groups in this chamber which are independent of party politics. There should be an expression by one spokesman at least representing the independent groups. I think we
Rules of the House

will be well advised to make provision in the proposed new rule for an expression of opinion on behalf of the independent groups, that in that respect they should be placed on a parity with the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Personally I have
no objection to limiting the time of speeches, but there may possibly be occasions when a man would need a longer period than forty minutes. I am inclined to think that a rule of this kind is rather an advantage, but I would agree very largely with the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in objecting to the exceptions that we have here. The proposed rule states that the leader of the opposition may have longer than forty minutes, and furthermore that the man who immediately follows the minister may have longer than forty minutes. Now as matters are arranged in this House the man that follows the minister is usually a member of the official opposition. That is not a fixed, written rule, but it is more or less a practice of the House, so that it means that almost invariably the official opposition, as it is known, has an opportunity of prolonging the speaking as long as may be necessary. That is a real discrimination against other sections of this House. We who belong to the smaller groups might very well make a plea for a little longer time proportionately than would in the ordinary way come to us. We recognize that there are certain territories, like the Yukon, or districts rather remote which, because of their peculiar character, because their population is scattered, find it necessary to have more than their proper proportion of representation. It would be quite possible for the opposition with its eighty or ninety members to say over and over again eighty or ninety times what its leader has said, whereas in the case of us who represent smaller groups, sometimes with only three or four in a group, we have only three or four men to express a viewpoint that may represent a considerable section of the public outside.
According to this rule there is an official recognition of the opposition, of parties in this House, and I do not think that is travelling along very good lines. If we are to have an exemption made in the case of the leader of the opposition, there ought also to be exemptions made in the case of representatives of other groups, and in saying that I do not forget that there are individuals like the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassal who have an equal right, with even a small

group, to represent in this House the particular point of view which they hold. Under these circumstances the only fair way would be to remove the exceptions. It may be said that because the Prime Minister or a minister introducing a government order is in an official position in the administration, an exception ought clearly to be made in his case. But that again is recognizing a wrong principle. It is very well for the government to have charge of the administration, but in matters of legislation the government already occupies too influential a position in this House. It is well known to hon. members that under existing practices it is almost impossible for a private member to introduce a bill with any hope that it will have an opportunity of coming before and being discussed by the House. On account of the regulations the bill goes down into an inferior position from which it rarely reappears. That is a wrong practice. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) to-night used the phrase "a mere member."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Private member

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not like the
term "a mere private member." I take it that the mere private member who is elected to this House has just as much right to introduce legislation as the Prime Minister himself. I say that without reflecting in the slightest on the Prime Minister or the government. As we come up from our various constituencies we have all equal rights in this House, and no rule ought to be introduced which would discriminate against any one member simply because he does not choose to associate himself with one of the larger groups.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How long
would the hon. member expect the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, representing, as he does, only himself in this House, to speak?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not speaking for the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think the House of Commons in this case is being compelled much against the wishes of many hon. members, to take some action to limit debate. No doubt the majority of the members would much prefer that each member should control himself and not make too long speeches in this House. If that were done we would not require any rule to curtail debate. It might be a good idea if we had a rule that when any hon. member had spoken for more than forty minutes, the Speaker would get up and read to him the resolution which the hon. member for Comox-Albemi quoted, and which

Rules of the House
was passed by the House some years ago protesting against long speeches. A few years ago I put on the order paper a proposal that we should have a time-keeper who would mark down the time occupied by every member speaking in this House or in committee of the whole, and that when a member had taken up say three hours in speeches during a session, his name should be handed to the Speaker and he should not be recognized by the Speaker if any other member wished to speak. This forty-minute rule is very drastic, but at the same time the House of Commons must adopt some measure of restriction of freedom of speech, because prior to this year we have had members who would speak for more than three hours. We have had leaders of the great parties in this House occupying as much as three hours. I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to the rule which is in force in the United States congress. It reads:
No member shall occupy more than one hour in debate on any question in the House or in committee.

speechtext:
They hand in their

There is another exception made of a member who makes a motion of "no confidence" in the government. The only free lance in the whole House, therefore, if this amendment goes through, will be the member who gets up and moves a want of confidence motion in the government, and it is a good job that that freedom is not being taken away from the average member. I do not think I would be in favour of this amendment if you removed these exceptions. I do not think I would be in favour of it if you increased the time limit from forty to fifty minutes. I believe the extra ten minutes would make a great difference, however. I do not see how you can
Rules of the House

mathematically figure out a speech that will take just forty minutes to deliver. If you devote ten minutes to your introduction and ten minutes to your conclusion you have only twenty minutes left for your development- not really long enough-and then instead of having actual growth of thought upwards you would have just the opposite-an arbitrary development rendered incomplete and ineffective on account of the time restriction.
So far as the time limit is concerned, I do not think we ought to put any time limit on the average member. I think it is the number of speakers we have in this House rather than the length of speeches that runs away with the time of the House. That is my opinion; hon. gentlemen can have theirs. Then there is the question of interruptions. I believe that an interruption is all right, but it should be made with the idea of getting information, and not simply to waste time or block the business of the House, which is the purpose of many interruptions. I do not believe we could have an up to date House of Commons unless we allowed interruptions and a certain amount of cross-firing. I believe that the present method of discussion and debate is the correct method, and if you simply have a member getting up and making a prepared speech, and no interruptions or questions are allowed, you will then have a dead House of Commons.
There is another idea, which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned, though not in quite the same way in which I prefer looking at what I regard as this curtailment of free speech. We talk about representative government and democracy, but what are the facts? We have sent to this House 245 members, and from among those 245 members a cabinet, a committee of the House, is chosen. That committee of the House has the power to initiate legislation, and there is where its great power lies. It has the power to direct, to guidte, but the development of the last century has brought about a situation where the cabinet-regardless of the party in power-our main committee of the House, instead of leading and guiding rationally, dominates, and I do not believe that any committee of the House should dominate. The big thing for us to do to-day is to preserve for the people of Canada responsible and representative government on the part of private members, and as the hon.

member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, I believe there will be a reaction in the country if we put this amendment through here to-night, and before a year goes by there will be a demand to have this new rule changed. If we are going to go on in that way, instead of having a white dial on the clock we shall need all the colours of the rainbow-green, blue, red and yellow-to tel us when to stop. The rights of a private member are to-day very largely limited. We are to a certain extent looked upon as ciphers in this parliament. We do not want that to go any further, and I am enough of a Liberal and a democrat to stand up here and say that I will not stand for it, and I am going to vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

What is the use of appointing a committee to revise the rules of the House if we are entirely to overlook and ignore the outstanding features of this parliament as it exists today? One of the most fruitful sources of disharmony in this House for the last five or six jrnars has been the existence of a third group. I do not object to the manner in which the rules have been applied in the past, because rules exist to be applied, but the necessary result of their application did not lead to the despatch of parliamentary work but rather to the contrary, and now that we are revising the rules why cannot we frankly face the fact that instead of two parties in this House we now have three or four? Surely if our object is to facilitate the business of the House we must so adapt out rules as to take into account all the factors which enter into that business, and I want to say that I do not know how this provision got into the rule. I must have been absent from the committee at the time, because I certainly would have been remiss in my duty had I let this go in without registering some objection. It is surely a very bold disregard of the presence of a third or fourth group in this House, that these words should be placed in such a rule, and I should think

Concessions are made along these lines frequently and I think in the revision of these rules the existence of a third point of view in the House should be recognized. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with all due respect I would move the amendment, but perhaps before doing so I might say something else which has occurred to me. I listened very attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), and I think he was entirely sincere in the attitude he took. We have had sufficient incidents of a serious character in our parliamentary development to justify fully any member being on his guard against any restriction of the right of private members. Therefore I concede to the hon. member and others who feel the same way a real sincerity of motive, and I think only that the occasion was somewhat mistaken by them. Personally I think that unrestricted freedom of speech is not the defence of free speech, as we have often seen in the course of the last five or six years; It is rather an abuse of free speech. I know it is a regrettable thing that rules have to be invoked in order even apparently to restrict free speech. It surely was a regrettable thing when the action of Parnell and his associates compelled the invoking of the closure, it was a regrettable event in the otherwise free development of British parliamentary experience. I think this also is a somewhat regrettable step to take, but the step has been made necessary by the wholesale abuse of the right of speech in this House in the last few years. After all I think that a step of this kind, which apparently has the fairly unanimous backing of the House is just a matter of self defence on the part of the greater majority of parliamentarians. As a matter of fact the ones who transgress are the few. The ones who impose themr selves upon us in the name of free speech are only a very insignificant proportion of the total membership of the House, and why should we be willing quiescently to submit from time to time to the false imposition of these gentlemen? Why cannot we agree on some rule that will bring these men to time? We have no other way of doing it. If we do not do that we are defenceless. It reminds me of a story in parliamentary history. On one occasion a well know parliamentarian was listening to a very long and tiresome speech. He happened to see another member with an ear trumpet to his ear, and he said to his neighbour: "There is a man throwing away his natural advantages." Well, Mr. Chairman, we have not very many natural advantages in this House when it comes to

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think it should be the "leader of the opposition."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not see why we should recognize one or two persons who call themselves a group or a political group. I am not very much moved by the appeal of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat in regard to groups, bearing in mind that he "inadvertently" voted against the very group that he belongs to.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think it is only fair to
give an explanation of how the committee was guided in this matter. A strong appeal was made to us that an opportunity should be afforded the three parties in this House to express their views. Generally when the government brings down the budget the
official opposition moves an amendment, and from time immemorial only one amendment has been allowed on going into committee of supply. Now hon. members will find at the top of page 26 a new rule which provides for a subamendment. There is to be one amendment, and one subamendment,[DOT] which is designed to afford the members independent of the two large parties the opportunity of making known their views. The present situation in that regard had been a bone of contention for the last four or five years in parliament, and we had some trouble on one or two occasions as to which of thd two groups was to be the opposition. I think this concession to the independent members will furnish them with the opportunity of moving, before going into committee of supply, a subamendment in which their own views can be stated fully. This concession was accepted as a compromise by the members of the committee. It is a departure from the practice of the House, but the committee agreed to recognize to that extent the three existing parties.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was very much interested to-night in hearing the hon. leader of the United Farmers of Alberta group- I think that is what he is styled-claim that he was opposed to any opposition or recognized opposition. Then we hear the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) suggesting that the members in that corner are the opposition, and bringing in an amendment. What I want to know is just where these hon. members stand? Are they in opposition or what are they? This amendment would lead us to believe that the various groups ;n that corner are in opposition, and the hon. gentleman virtually says so in his amendment.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is well known that the term is applied to those members who do not sit on the government benches. There was no implication in the use of the word that we were anything like an official opposition.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You always refer to the members sitting in front of me-Mr. Neiil and Mr. Bourassa-as "independents." You have not included them. We want to know where this outfit stands.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman surely
is attributing to us motives that it is not proper to attribute to us at all. Because we sit on this side and sometimes express independent criticism does not imply that we are the only opposition. The hon. gentleman seems to want to put us-

Will my hon. friend
permit me? Can he tell us himself how many would be entitled to the longer speech if his amendment carries?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
For all practical purposes I
admit frankly that it might extend on occasions to three or four, but even at that I think the House could very well make a concession for the sake of good will. While I am on my feet I want to say something in regard to a remark passed by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I do not wish to bring up anything that is past or dead, or that should be so regarded, but I do not intend to sit here calmly and listen to the insinuations that the hon. member for Frontenac has made on one or two oocasions respecting an action of mine. I think it would be becoming of him and his colleagues on that side of the House if they would let that incident drop. During the election he and others sitting on the front benches went out of their way to spread from one constituency to another statements that not one of them would dare to make on the floor of this House, that not one of them would be man enough to make to my face.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think it is descending to a very low level of parliamentary practice for the hon. gentleman with his experience to stand up and make those base insinuations about the action of another member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The remarks of the
hon. gentleman are not relevant to the matter which is before the committee.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: They may not be relevant, but I think as a member of this House-

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I rise to
a point of order. Is it within the rules for an hon. member to accuse another of making base insinuations? I do not think it is.
I am sorry indeed if he or anyone else is accusing me of making insinuations. What I stated were facts. I do not bother wasting my time with making insinuations.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It does not make the matter any different for the hon. member to use his subtlety of mind to get himself out of a situation which no self-respecting member would place himself in.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: No self-respecting member would be guilty of the inadvertence which he committed.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OP REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I move a certain amendment to the amendment which I think will make the matter clear? I move:

That the new rule to be added after rule 21 be replaced by the paragraph:
.No speech delivered in the House of Commons shall be recorded in Hansard."
